analysis.one_liner: Restores the DEA's power to quickly freeze suspicious opioid shipments from drug companies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in two House subcommittees until Congress ended, despite a Republican lead sponsor and 15 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2016, Congress passed a law that made it harder for the Drug Enforcement Administration to immediately freeze shipments from drug companies it suspected of feeding the opioid epidemic. This bill would repeal that 2016 law and restore the stricter enforcement standard the DEA used before. It was introduced in October 2017 with a bipartisan group of backers, but neither committee it was assigned to ever took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities hit hard by opioid overdoses, and the DEA itself, which would regain the authority to move quickly against distributors and manufacturers whose shipments feed the black market.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Public Law 114-145 (the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act of 2016) in full, effective as if it had never been enacted.

Repealing the 2016 law restores the provisions of sections 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act as they read before the amendment, restoring the DEA's authority to carry out enforcement actions in drug diversion control investigations and operations to combat the opioid epidemic.

The bill's stated purpose is to ensure the DEA has the authority it needs for enforcement actions against drug diversion, in the middle of an epidemic that was killing tens of thousands of Americans a year.

analysis.who_pays: Drug wholesale distributors, opioid manufacturers, and pharmacies, which would again face the risk of DEA immediate suspension orders and fines if their shipments looked suspicious; some pain patients could face supply disruption if the DEA acts aggressively against a supplier they depend on.

drawbacks.text: The 2016 law was deliberately titled the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act; its stated aim was to balance enforcement against patient access, and an honest supporter of repeal should acknowledge that restoring the old standard could let the DEA cut off legitimate opioid supply to pharmacies and patients if it overreaches.

The bill is a wholesale repeal rather than a redesign: it restores the pre-2016 standard exactly as written, rather than recalibrating the immediate-suspension process or adding due-process protections.
Restoring DEA enforcement tools addresses the supply side of the epidemic only; it does not, by itself, fund addiction treatment or prevention.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and specific: the DEA gets back the authority it had before 2016 to freeze suspicious opioid shipments, which is the tool the agency's own former officials said they lost at the height of the epidemic. The costs are real but manageable — the risk of overbroad suspensions cutting off legitimate patients, and the loss of the access protections the 2016 law's drafters said they intended. A more carefully drafted bill might have preserved both, but this one at least does what it says cleanly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and then to two subcommittees, and neither ever held a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The RESTORE Act of 2017 was introduced on October 19, 2017 by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick and referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Judiciary Committee.

On October 20, 2017 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and on November 1, 2017 to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations.
The bill's only cosponsor list shows 15 members: 11 Democrats and 4 Republicans.
After the November 1 subcommittee referral, the record shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019.
The bill would have repealed Public Law 114-145, the 2016 law that weakened the DEA's immediate-suspension authority over controlled-substance shipments.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug wholesale distributors and opioid manufacturers came out ahead: the 2016 law they benefited from stayed on the books, and the DEA kept the weaker standard for freezing their shipments. The committee chairs who never scheduled action were never forced to explain on the record.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — the lead sponsor was a Republican and the cosponsors split 11 Democrats to 4 Republicans — and no vote was ever taken, so no party-line breakdown exists.

industries.note: The 2016 law raised the bar the DEA had to meet before it could immediately suspend a distributor's shipments and subpoena its records; this bill restores the stricter pre-2016 standard, exposing distributors again to shipment freezes and fines. Because the bill died, the 2016-law protections remained in place.

Restored section 303 of the Controlled Substances Act applies to manufacturers as well, so repeal would have exposed factories and recordkeeping to suspension orders if DEA found a substantial threat to public safety. The bill never advanced, so their position under the 2016 law was unchanged.

industries.industry: Pharmacies and dispensers of controlled substances
industries.note: Dispensers fall under the same registration provisions, so repeal would increase their risk of DEA action; but the 2016 law's access protections also benefited pain patients who rely on pharmacies for legitimate prescriptions, which is the trade-off repeal supporters had to weigh.
